meaning.text: The domovoy is given the name bannik because, besides the hut, he settles in bath-houses (wherever a stove is built).
When the domovoy haunts a bath (banya), he is known as a Bannik.

scene.text: Late hours of the night in the bath.
Behind the stove or under the steaming shelf of the bath.
His whistling, laughter and howling are often heard from behind the stove or under the shelf.

behavior_habitat.text: The bannik lives behind the stove or under the steaming shelf of the bath.
The bannik does not like people who bathe (steam themselves) at night.
The bannik often suffocates (strangles) those who bathe at night.
This happens especially if the bathers have not said a prayer before washing.

dealing_with_it.text: The peasants avoid staying in the bath at late hours, because of the bannik.
In the Smolensk Government, people climbing onto the shelf to steam say: "The baptised onto the shelf, the unbaptised off the shelf!"
In the Smolensk Government, peasants leaving the bath leave a bucket of water and a whisk (besom) for the domovoy, so that he too can wash and steam himself.

origin.text: Afanasyev holds that the domovoy settles in baths as well as the hut, wherever a stove is built, and is therefore called bannik.
Afanasyev holds that when separate bath-houses and corn-kilns came to be built, the domovoy received new names, and these gave rise to the idea of special spirits in charge of these outbuildings.

rationale.text: Every surviving clause is for one people, the Russians; the only region named is the Smolensk Government.
Only two sources name the bannik: Afanasyev (1868) and Ralston (1872).

Ralston is not independent of Afanasyev here: his Domovoy section cites Afanasyev ("says Afanasief", P. V. S. ii. 67) two pages before the bannik passage, and his bannik lore follows Afanasyev pp.69-70 point for point (bath, night bathers suffocated, no prayer, corn-kiln, Smolensk bucket and whisk).

Counted by author, the entry rests on one 19th-century compiler, Afanasyev, who himself presents the bannik as the domovoy under a new name and holds that such names produced the idea of separate outbuilding spirits; so the grade is literary rather than regional.

sources.author: W. R. S. Ralston
sources.title: The Songs of the Russian People

sources.author: А. Н. Афанасьев (A. N. Afanasyev)
sources.title: Поэтические воззрения славян на природу, т. 2

notes.text: appearance: no source describes the bannik's body or form; searched bannik, Bannilc, банник, банникъ, баннаго, банный, банн, бан-, banya, баня, банѣ, бани, в бане, bath, bath-room, bath-house, bath-spirit, bannick, баенник, байник, подовинник, бања, Badstube across all sources (bath also scoped to ralston1872, ralston1873 and machal1918). Only ralston1872:p.123 and afanasyev1868:pp.69-70 name the bannik.
variants: no source distinguishes the bannik by people or region beyond the single Smolensk Government custom, which is recorded in dealing_with_it; searched the same terms.

Both sources present the bannik as the domovoy when he lives in the bath, not as a separate being (ralston1872:p.123 'When he haunts a bath (banya) he is known as a Bannik'; afanasyev1868:p.69). The Smolensk bucket-and-whisk custom is stated on both pages for 'the domovoy' leaving the bath, in the bannik paragraph; the clause keeps the word domovoy. The relation to domovoi is set to 'related'; 'instance-of' may be the better reading and is left for verify.

Not used: machal1918:p.241 describes the domovoy 'in the bath-room' (creeps under the benches, hissing, rumbling, giggling; a pail of water made ready for him) but never names the bannik. afanasyev1869:p.310 says that in the Novgorod Government the theft of infants is ascribed to 'domestic spirits living in bath-houses', where women are taken to wash after childbirth; the page does not name the bannik, so it is left out. afanasyev1869:p.137 (an old woman living 'in the bath or in the bushes', southern Siberia) is about the poludnitsa, not the bannik.

names.variants: 'баннаго' is printed in the genitive ('названия баннаго (банника)'); the form is kept exactly as printed and romanised letter for letter, not normalised to a nominative. Ralston's 'Bannilc' (ralston1872:p.123) is an OCR misreading of 'Bannik', printed correctly two lines later, and is not listed as a variant.
